subject: Critical Thinking
title: Framing: How the Same Facts Tell Different Stories
description: One-minute skill: Framing: How the Same Facts Tell Different Stories.

hook.text: '95% fat-free' and '5% fat' are the same fact. But one sells yogurt and the other doesn't. That's framing.

buildup.text: Framing: presenting information in a way that influences interpretation without changing the facts.

discovery.text: Tversky & Kahneman: 'A surgery with a 90% survival rate' vs. 'a 10% mortality rate.' Same data, very different choices.

twist.text: Every news headline is a frame. 'Protesters clash with police' vs.

climax.text: Reframe to defend: when someone frames an issue, restate the same facts in the opposite frame.

punchline.text: Same facts, different frame, different conclusion.

quiz.question: What is framing in argumentation?
options: Presenting the same facts in a way that influences how they're interpreted
Making up facts to support a conclusion

details.summary: Framing presents the same information through different lenses to influence interpretation. A surgery with a 90% survival rate sounds safer than one with a 10% mortality rate, even though they are identical.
details.whyItMatters: Framing shapes opinions in politics, media, and marketing. Recognizing frames helps you evaluate information on its merits rather than its presentation.
takeaways: Framing changes perception without changing facts
Positive and negative frames trigger different decisions
Every news headline is a framing choice

faq.question: How can you detect framing in news reporting?
faq.answer: Compare how different outlets cover the same event. Notice word choices, what details are prominent versus buried, and whether the headline emphasizes gains or losses. Different frames reveal editorial bias.

faq.question: Why does framing affect decisions even when people know the facts?
faq.answer: Framing exploits System 1 emotional processing that operates automatically. Even when you understand both frames intellectually, the emotional weight of the frame still influences your intuitive response.
